transcript.content: Hello, I’m glad you came in. What brings you in today?

Hi. Well, I guess what finally pushed me to make this appointment is that I'm having a really hard time staying focused at work. 

I manage a clinic, and I can sit down to run an EPIC quality report, or go into a metrics meeting with every intention of tracking what's going on. But within just a few minutes, my mind has drifted so far off that I realize I'm just rereading the exact same numbers over and over. Or I'll suddenly realize I completely missed the whole point of the discussion. It's just getting really frustrating.
Have you had trouble paying attention like this since you were a child?

Yes, I have. Even back in elementary school, I remember... well, my teachers would always write on my report cards that I was bright but careless. And my mother actually had to sit right there with me while I finished my homework. If she didn't, I would just lose track of the assignments, or I'd realize I completely forgot to bring my books home from school. So, yes, it's been going on for a long time.
Do you often feel restless or like you have to fidget or move around when you’re supposed to stay still?

No, not really. I don't have a problem sitting still. I can sit at my desk or in those long meetings without feeling like I need to get up or move around. It's really just my mind that wanders off, not my body.
Over the past couple of weeks, have you been feeling down or depressed most of the day?
No, I wouldn't say I've been feeling down or depressed. I mean, I get frustrated with myself at work when I can't focus, but it's not a sad or depressed feeling. My mood is generally fine.
Do you often find yourself feeling very anxious or worried most days?

No, I wouldn't say that. I mean, my job can be stressful sometimes, but I don't feel anxious or worried on a daily basis. It's really just the usual stress of falling behind when I lose track of things, not an everyday kind of anxiety.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient has a longstanding pattern of inattention beginning in childhood, with persistent difficulty sustaining focus, careless errors/losing track of tasks, and academic impairment requiring parental support. Hyperactivity/impulsivity symptoms are denied, and there is no evidence that the symptoms are better explained by depression or anxiety. This is most consistent with attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder, predominantly inattentive presentation.
